30: When departing an aerodrome without an operating control tower, you must comply with the traffic pattern established for that aerodrome (RAAC 91 / FAR 91.127). Left turns are only the fallback default when no pattern is published. Departing in any direction ignores the pattern, so (a) is wrong; (b) states only the default, not the governing rule.
71: Under RAAC 91.151(a)(1), for VFR to a destination with no alternate you need fuel to fly to the intended landing point plus a reserve (30% of the leg time) that must never be less than 45 minutes. That is option (c). The 30-minute figure in (b) is the FAA day-VFR rule, not the Argentine requirement.
80: The seat belt and the shoulder harness are both required for crew members at their stations during takeoff and landing (RAAC 91.105). En route, only the seat belt must stay fastened while at the station; the harness is not required for the whole operation. Since the question asks about belt AND harness together, the answer is takeoff and landing, not the entire flight.
93: Passengers must be told to fasten their seat belts before surface movement (taxi), takeoff and landing (RAAC 91.106(a)(2)). There is no rule requiring belts for the entire flight, so 'during the whole flight' is wrong. Turbulence is a recommendation, not the rule's defined phases.
99:
Load factor in a level turn is n = 1/cos(bank). At 45°, n = 1/0.707 = 1.414 (also shown in the Figure 2 table).
2200 kg x 1.414 = 3111 kg, so about 3100 kg (b). 3300 kg would require n = 1.5, which does not correspond to 45°.
100:
Crosswind component = wind speed x sin(angle off the runway), so max wind = crosswind / sin(angle).
25 / sin 45° = 25 / 0.707 = 35.4 kt, about 35 kt (c). On Figure 37 the 45° radial meets the 25 kt crosswind line between the 30 and 40 kt arcs. 25 kt would only be right for a 90° wind.
101: Atmospheric stability is determined by comparing the temperature of a displaced parcel of air with the temperature of the surrounding air (lapse rate vs. environment). If the parcel is warmer than its surroundings it keeps rising (unstable); if cooler it sinks back (stable). Pressure difference does not define stability, and turbulence is only a symptom of instability, not how it is determined.
123: Under the right-of-way rules (RAAC 91.113 / ICAO Annex 2 3.2.2.3), power-driven aircraft must give way to aircraft seen to be towing another aircraft or object. An airship has priority over a gyroplane, but the aircraft towing a glider has priority over both, so (c) is correct.
126:
Wind 180° at 20 kt. Crosswind = 20 x sin(angle between wind and runway).
Rwy 10 (100°): 80° off, 20 x sin80° = 19.7 kt. Rwy 24 (240°): 60° off, 20 x sin60° = 17.3 kt. Rwy 14 (140°): 40° off, 20 x sin40° = 12.9 kt.
Only Rwy 14 stays within the 13 kt limit (Figure 37 gives the same readings), so the answer is (b).
140: In VMC the pilot may fly under VFR or, if desired, under IFR, so 'always VFR' is false. Special VFR applies below VMC minima, so (a) is wrong. RAAC 91 states that in VMC the pilot remains directly responsible for avoiding collisions with other aircraft, even when flying IFR under an ATC clearance, which is the point of (c).
141: For flights planned as controlled from the start, RAAC 91 requires the flight plan to be filed at least 45 minutes before the estimated off-block time (EOBT). The question reproduces that wording, so the answer is 45 minutes (c). 60 minutes is the ICAO default and is not the figure in the rule the item is based on.
156: In Figure 67 the wind blows toward the top, so turn 4-5-6 begins heading into the wind at low groundspeed. That turn should start with a shallow bank and steepen gradually. If the bank is increased too rapidly early in the turn, the half-circle comes out smaller and the turn is not completed before reaching the reference line (b). Slow bank increase late in the turn (c) would instead widen the arc.
169: Flying from low to high pressure without resetting the altimeter: the setting stays at the lower value, so the instrument under-reads. It indicates LOWER than actual altitude (c). Memory aid: 'High to low, look out below' (high to low pressure makes the altimeter over-read, the opposite case).
256: In the Aeronautical Decision-Making DECIDE model, the first step is Detect: noticing that a change has occurred that requires attention. Identify, Estimate/Evaluate and the later steps come after detection. Thus 'detectarlo' (b) is the first step in the decision-making process.
262:
1) Pressure altitude: the Figure 8 table gives 673 ft at 29.2 and 579 ft at 29.3, so about 626 ft at 29.25. PA = 5250 + 626 = 5876 ft.
2) Enter the chart at 81°F (about 27°C) and follow up to the 5876 ft PA line: density altitude is about 8500 ft (c).
5877 ft is only the pressure altitude, not the density altitude. Check: ISA at 5900 ft is about 3°C, 24°C warmer than standard, 120 ft x 24 = 2900 ft added, giving about 8700 ft.
266: On a 2-bar VASI, red over white means on the glide path. In illustration A the far (upper) bar is red above the white near bar, so the aircraft is on the glide path (b). Both bars red means below the glide path; both white means above.
268: RAAC 91.156 sets the VFR minimums in the traffic zone of an aerodrome outside a control zone at 2500 m visibility and a 1000 ft ceiling (c). 5 km and 1000 ft applies to controlled aerodromes and aerodromes within a control zone, and 8 km applies to VFR en-route flight.
276:
1) Pressure altitude: the Figure 8 table gives -348 at 30.3 and -440 at 30.4, so -394 ft at 30.35. PA = 3894 - 394 = 3500 ft.
2) At 25°F (about -4°C) on the 3500 ft PA line, the chart gives a density altitude of about 2000 ft (a).
Check: ISA at 3500 ft is about +8°C, so the air is about 12°C colder than standard, and 12 x 120 = about -1400 ft, giving roughly 2100 ft. 3500 ft is only the pressure altitude.
307:
Max wind = crosswind component / sin(wind angle).
25 kt / sin 45° = 25 / 0.707 = 35.4 kt, about 35 kt. On the wind component chart the 45° radial crosses the 25 kt crosswind line at about 35 kt total wind. 25 kt would only apply to a 90° wind.
319: Wind 040° at 10 kt would favour Rwy 04, but the figure shows Rwy 04/22 closed (X at both ends), so it cannot be used. Rwy 18 would give a tailwind. Rwy 36 is 40° off the wind: headwind 10 x cos40° = 7.7 kt, crosswind 10 x sin40° = 6.4 kt. The correct runway is 36 (b).
327: Hypoxia is oxygen deficiency affecting the brain and other organs. For optimum protection, pilots should avoid flying above 10,000 ft MSL for prolonged periods without supplemental oxygen (c). 10,000 m (about 33,000 ft) is far too high, and 1,000 m is far too low to cause hypoxia.
355: When hand-propping an engine, it is extremely important that a competent pilot be at the controls in the cockpit, so the aircraft is controlled (brakes, throttle, mixture, ignition) if the engine starts. Option (a) alone is a callout, not a substitute for having a competent pilot at the controls, and (c) leaves out the essential point: being at the controls.
371: A mixture that is too lean burns hot and unevenly, raising cylinder temperatures and causing detonation (c). Black smoke and red flames in the exhaust are signs of an over-rich mixture, not a lean one. A lean mixture does not increase power; it can lead to overheating and engine damage.
375: Higher temperature, higher humidity or lower pressure raise density altitude, meaning thinner air. The engine takes in less air mass, so power output drops, and the propeller bites less air, so propeller efficiency drops as well. Both fall considerably (c). 'Only propeller efficiency' (b) is wrong because engine power also decreases.
